extracted.intended_audience: factory owners, engineers, occupational health practitioners, and informed general readers interested in industrial hygiene
extracted.subtask_description: Practical recommendations and principles for preventing occupational poisoning and respiratory disease in manufacturing — covering classification of airborne hazards, personal and process protections, medical antidotes, substitution, and ventilation/machinery remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of airborne industrial hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide cases of contamination of the air by insalubrious industrial operations into two groups: (1) emanations (dusts or vapors) that act as poisons and, carried by the blood to all parts of the body, produce general and various disorders; (2) dusts of a simply irritating character which act locally on the lungs and produce disorders depending on particle hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also subdivide irritating dusts into those insoluble in bodily fluids (which accumulate in the lungs and obstruct them) and those soluble (which have only transient effects). This classification guides choice of preventive measures and prognosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of protective veils / masks to arrest inhalation
rubrics_metrics.description: The most obvious precaution is to arrest the passage of poisonous dusts with a protective veil or mask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective and convenient masks exist (examples: wadded masks in Belgian mines; thin silken veil with spectacles for millstone workers). Note practical barriers: workers often resist wearing screens; adoption may require persuasion or management enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special work clothing and control of clothing contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers in hazardous processes (e.g., white-lead) ought to wear special clothing for their work; mere overalls over ordinary clothes are insufficient because they allow transport of dust by the clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide dedicated work garments and laundering/bathing facilities to prevent carry‑home contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal hygiene measures: baths and cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleanliness and personal hygiene (including baths) are important preventive measures against occupational poisoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts to introduce baths have met resistance (example: workers quitting rather than using a bath-room), so implementation must consider worker acceptance and facilities design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit eating or storing food in shops
rubrics_metrics.description: Workmen should never deposit or eat their food in the shop, or allow it to be exposed to mixture with poisonous dusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an essential personal-hygiene rule to prevent ingestion of toxic particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical antidotes and prophylactics (iodide of potassium, milk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antidotes and preventive ingestibles have been recommended: iodide of potassium (Meisens, 1843) used with excellent effect for lead and mercury; milk recommended (Didier-Jean, 1867) as a preventive for lead-poisoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iodide of potassium cured declared lead diseases (e.g., paralysis) and permitted continued work; milk was suggested but workers may reject it or substitute alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression and removal of dusts at source
rubrics_metrics.description: General hygienic measures include suppression of dust generation (produce as little as possible) and removal of dusts as soon as they are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: moistening, grinding and mixing under water, closed apparatus for pulverizing, natural and artificial ventilation, substitution of machines for hand labor, and mechanical packing. Example: white-lead made ground in oil produced far less dust and far fewer sicknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of inoffensive substances for toxic compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, replace poisonous compounds (e.g., lead, quicksilver) with less harmful alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: zinc-white or sulphuret of zinc as rivals for white-lead; lime- and manganese-based glazes as substitutes for lead oxide in pottery; aniline-derived colors (eosine, fluorescine) for children's toys. Substitution may face objections (e.g., perceived inferior coloring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering controls: machinery to remove human exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce machinery to perform the most insalubrious phases of work so as to eliminate direct human exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: replacement of gilding with mercury by galvanoplasty; silvering of glass by safer plating processes; mechanization of match manufacture to avoid phosphorous inhalation. Division of labor and mechanization reduce exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active ventilation to carry off vapors and dusts
rubrics_metrics.description: Energetic natural or artificial ventilation is essential to remove poisonous vapors and airborne dusts from work areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certain volatile toxins (sulphide of carbon, phosphorus vapors), ventilation is the primary practical control when closed apparatus is not used. Work with highly volatile substances should be limited to large well‑ventilated establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local chemical controls and sprays for mercury
rubrics_metrics.description: For mercury hazards, employ ammoniacal sprays in shops and iodide of potassium as remedies/preventives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures were recommended after experiments and have been used with excellent effect; combine with division of labor and ventilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed handling for volatile softening agents (sulphide of carbon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle sulphide of carbon only in closed vessels or with enclosures that prevent vapor escape; otherwise ensure active ventilation and limit such work to large well-ventilated establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example apparatus: glass box with hand openings and rubber sleeves to work without vapor outlet — often rejected by workers, so ventilation remains critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of siliceous and coal dusts to prevent chronic lung disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent accumulation of insoluble dusts (coal, silica) in pulmonary vesicles to avoid anthracosis and other fatal diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls include wadded masks (success in Belgian mines), projection of water ('rain') to settle dust, and substitution of inoffensive dusting agents (fecula, talc) in iron-founding. Protective veils and eye protection are recommended for millstone and porcelain workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local neutralizers for specific vapors (phosphorus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutralize harmful vapors locally when possible (e.g., essence of turpentine in a bottle hung about the neck to neutralize phosphoric vapors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an interim measure; ultimate control is suppression of vapors by mechanization or enclosing dangerous steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address behavioral resistance to protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Worker attitudes and habits (carelessness, refusal to use protective devices, preference for alcoholic drinks over milk) are key obstacles to implementing hygienic measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful programs must account for cultural and behavioral barriers; technological fixes alone may fail if workers reject them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate dust hazard severity by particle properties and solubility
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensity of lung disorders from dust generally depends on the hardness and solubility of particles: insoluble (siliceous) dusts accumulate and cause irreparable harm; soluble dusts have transient effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical distinction should guide prioritization of protections and medical prognosis (e.g., St. Roch disease described for siliceous dust victims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer process redesign and industrial-scale accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where individual protective devices are impractical, redesign processes (closed apparatus, wet methods) and concentrate hazardous work in large, well-ventilated establishments with appropriate machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: centralizing sulphide of carbon operations in large plants; adoption of wet grinding and closed pulverizers; the General Match Company mechanizing the mixing, dipping, and packing to eliminate exposure.
